source.title: Micro Batch Streaming: Allowing the Training of DNN models Using a large batch size on Small Memory Systems
source.authors: DoangJoo Synn; Xin-Yu Piao; Jooyoung Park; Jong-Kook Kim

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, although its tables are represented only by captions and narrative descriptions; exact table entries are unavailable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares classification or segmentation performance across effective mini-batch sizes, using micro-batch gradient accumulation to test whether larger batches change performance.
record.gate_note: Reports performance results for different mini-batch sizes and compares MBP with training without MBP. The paper does not state that epoch budgets were held fixed, and it does not report the generalization gap as a train-versus-test difference.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates memory-efficient gradient accumulation and reports performance across batch sizes, but does not identify held-out evaluation data or establish equal epoch budgets. Its reported training performance and selected maximum accuracies cannot establish V5's held-out batch-size penalty or its removal. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that MBP enables larger effective batches on a single memory-limited GPU, with broadly comparable reported performance and improvements at selected batch sizes. They do not establish a fixed-epoch held-out generalization result.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sequential micro-batches with gradient accumulation and loss normalization to emulate a larger mini-batch; evaluates memory capacity and performance rather than the generalization gap under a stated fixed epoch budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported accuracy or IoU varies with mini-batch size; selected batch sizes yield higher performance, while overall performance is described as comparable.

fits_no_version.finding: MBP yields similar training curves at matched effective batch sizes and selected higher maximum accuracy or IoU values when exploring larger effective batches. Held-out evaluation and equal epoch budgets are not established.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Micro-batch gradient accumulation enables training beyond GPU batch-memory limits while preserving reported performance in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The introduction reports larger-batch improvements of 21.88% for ResNet-50 classification and 2.01% for U-Net segmentation on higher-resolution images, without identifying held-out evaluation or training budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reported task performance can improve with larger batches in these image-resolution comparisons.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the numeric entries of Tables 3–5, limiting row-level performance comparisons. It does not specify a fixed epoch budget or report the train-versus-test error gap.
record.rows_left_out: No further results were extracted. The per-size accuracy, IoU, and timing entries from Tables 3–5 are not present in the supplied text; Figure 5 is described qualitatively only.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width scaling beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
Held-out performance across effective batch sizes under established equal epoch budgets, including a large-batch penalty and its recovery through recipe changes.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with training–test gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Missing table entries are already declared in rows_left_out. Neither maximum accuracy nor the conclusion's general reference to testing establishes a held-out evaluation protocol.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Network width beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization comparisons.
The paper does not state a fixed epoch budget or compare language models. It evaluates larger batches enabled by MBP against batches that fit without MBP.
Dropout and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures of the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy at different mini-batch sizes using MBP and without MBP.
rows.baseline: 2.44% lower accuracy for the model without MBP
rows.note: The paper reports the difference but does not provide the absolute accuracy here.
rows.check: The 2.44% improvement is reported correctly, but accuracy is not identified as held-out. The comparator is training without MBP at an unspecified baseline batch size, not without MBP at batch size 128. This is a method-performance comparison, not an established V5 result.

rows.subject: ResNet-101
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy at different mini-batch sizes using MBP and without MBP.
rows.baseline: 2.32% lower accuracy for the model without MBP
rows.note: The paper reports the difference but does not provide the absolute accuracy here.
rows.check: The 2.32% improvement is reported correctly, but held-out evaluation and equal epoch budgets are unspecified. The baseline batch size is unavailable; this does not isolate a large-batch generalization effect.

rows.subject: AmoebaNet-D
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy at different mini-batch sizes using MBP and without MBP.
rows.baseline: 1.41% lower accuracy for the model without MBP
rows.note: The paper reports the difference but does not provide the absolute accuracy here.
rows.check: The 1.41% improvement at batch size 32 is stated, but the maximum accuracy is not identified as held-out. The baseline batch size and epoch budget are unspecified.

rows.subject: AmoebaNet-D
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy at different mini-batch sizes using MBP and without MBP.
rows.baseline: 1.29% lower accuracy for the model without MBP
rows.note: The paper reports comparable performance and states this difference; it does not provide absolute accuracy here.
rows.check: The 1.29% improvement at batch size 256 is stated, but held-out evaluation and equal epoch budgets are unspecified. Comparable method performance does not establish absence of V5's penalty.

rows.subject: U-Net
rows.operation_detail: Compared IoU at different mini-batch sizes using MBP and without MBP.
rows.note: The paper identifies 97.51% as the highest IoU and says it is 2.03% higher than the model without MBP.
rows.check: The 97.51% maximum IoU and reported 2.03% improvement are accurate. This is a segmentation result without an identified held-out split or equal epoch budget, outside V5's stated classifier and language-model comparison.
